title: Following Tracers Along Axons
endLine: Axon transport carries tracers to map connections; function takes separate tests.

scenes.tts: How do you map which neurons connect inside a tangled brain? A neuron's long output fibre, its axon, travels inside bundles called tracts. Because a neuron carries no label showing its partners, that wiring stays hidden.
scenes.caption: How do you map which neurons connect inside a tangled brain? A neuron's long output fibre, its axon, travels inside bundles called tracts. Because a neuron carries no label showing its partners, that wiring stays hidden.
scenes.visual: Schematic cross-section of nervous tissue filling most of the frame height: clusters of neuron cell bodies on the left and right linked by a dense central bundle of axons (a tract). A question mark pulses over the tangled tract while faint schematic vesicles drift along the fibres; one axon briefly brightens, carrying no label.
scenes.narration: How do you map which neurons connect inside a tangled brain? A neuron's long output fibre, its axon, travels inside bundles called tracts. Because a neuron carries no label showing its partners, that wiring stays hidden.

scenes.visual: The same schematic tissue dims slightly behind high-contrast title text: "Following Tracers Along Axons". Slow ambient schematic vesicles continue drifting along the central axon bundle.

scenes.tts: Neurons already move cargo along axons using their own transport machinery. Tract tracing puts visible dye onto that traffic. Inject biotinylated dextran amine near cell bodies in one region. Those neurons carry it forward toward their terminals. This forward mapping, called anterograde tracing, shows where those cells project.
scenes.caption: Neurons already move cargo along axons using their own transport machinery. Tract tracing puts visible dye onto that traffic. Inject biotinylated dextran amine near cell bodies in one region. Those neurons carry it forward toward their terminals. This forward mapping, called anterograde tracing, shows where those cells project.
scenes.visual: In the same schematic tissue cross-section, a fine pipette lowers into the left cell-body cluster and releases a glowing cyan pool labelled "biotinylated dextran amine". Bright packets ride forward left-to-right along the central tract until the axon terminals on the right glow. The label "Anterograde" appears after the terminals brighten.
scenes.narration: Neurons already move cargo along axons using their own transport machinery. Tract tracing puts visible dye onto that traffic. Inject biotinylated dextran amine near cell bodies in one region. Those neurons carry it forward toward their terminals. This forward mapping, called anterograde tracing, shows where those cells project.

scenes.tts: Axon transport also runs backward, from terminals to cell bodies. Inject Fluorogold into a target region instead. Terminals there absorb it and carry it back to distant cell bodies. That reverse route is retrograde tracing. Every tracer uses axon transport to turn hidden wiring into visible paths.
scenes.caption: Axon transport also runs backward, from terminals to cell bodies. Inject Fluorogold into a target region instead. Terminals there absorb it and carry it back to distant cell bodies. That reverse route is retrograde tracing. Every tracer uses axon transport to turn hidden wiring into visible paths.
scenes.visual: The cyan glow clears from the same schematic tissue. The pipette moves to the right target region and releases a glowing amber pool labelled "Fluorogold". Axon terminals absorb amber packets that travel backward right-to-left along the tract until the distant cell bodies on the left glow brightly. The label "Retrograde" appears once the cell bodies light up.
scenes.narration: Axon transport also runs backward, from terminals to cell bodies. Inject Fluorogold into a target region instead. Terminals there absorb it and carry it back to distant cell bodies. That reverse route is retrograde tracing. Every tracer uses axon transport to turn hidden wiring into visible paths.

scenes.tts: Now test that logic. Cholera toxin B subunit travels both ways along an axon. Suppose you inject it into a middle region, and a neighbouring region glows. From that bright patch alone, can you tell whether axons enter or leave?
scenes.caption: Now test that logic. Cholera toxin B subunit travels both ways along an axon. Suppose you inject it into a middle region, and a neighbouring region glows. From that bright patch alone, can you tell whether axons enter or leave?
scenes.visual: The same schematic tissue shifts to show a middle region connected by a tract to a neighbouring region. The pipette injects a gold pool labelled "cholera toxin B subunit" into the middle region. Schematic arrows pulse in both directions along the tract as the neighbouring region brightens into an ambiguous glowing patch beside the question card: "Do axons enter or leave?"
scenes.narration: Now test that logic. Cholera toxin B subunit travels both ways along an axon. Suppose you inject it into a middle region, and a neighbouring region glows. From that bright patch alone, can you tell whether axons enter or leave?

scenes.visual: The question "Do axons enter or leave?" stays on screen during the silent pause while faint bi-directional schematic pulses drift slowly along the tract between the middle and neighbouring regions.

scenes.tts: Not from the glow alone. Because cholera toxin B subunit travels both ways, researchers must establish direction for each tracer first. Dye injections carry a second limit. They mark cells or terminals taking up enough dye. That reveals population wiring, not one cell's synapses.
scenes.caption: Not from the glow alone. Because cholera toxin B subunit travels both ways, researchers must establish direction for each tracer first. Dye injections carry a second limit. They mark cells or terminals taking up enough dye. That reveals population wiring, not one cell's synapses.
scenes.visual: In the same schematic tissue, the ambiguous glowing patch splits into two clearly labelled test cases—"Incoming terminals" versus "Outgoing cell bodies"—showing why direction must be established first. The view widens back to the dye pool, where dozens of axons light up together as a crowd beneath the label "Population wiring only".
scenes.narration: Not from the glow alone. Because cholera toxin B subunit travels both ways, researchers must establish direction for each tracer first. Dye injections carry a second limit. They mark cells or terminals taking up enough dye. That reveals population wiring, not one cell's synapses.

scenes.tts: To pinpoint direct partners, researchers use genetically targeted viruses. A modified rabies virus starts in a defined starter population, or even one starter cell. Restricted to one synaptic step, it crosses one synapse back to label the neurons that feed it directly.
scenes.caption: To pinpoint direct partners, researchers use genetically targeted viruses. A modified rabies virus starts in a defined starter population, or even one starter cell. Restricted to one synaptic step, it crosses one synapse back to label the neurons that feed it directly.
scenes.visual: The glowing crowd of axons dims inside the same schematic tissue until one highlighted starter neuron stands out on the right. A schematic modified rabies marker begins inside that starter cell, jumps backward across exactly one synaptic gap, and lights up only the two directly presynaptic neurons on the left before stopping.
scenes.narration: To pinpoint direct partners, researchers use genetically targeted viruses. A modified rabies virus starts in a defined starter population, or even one starter cell. Restricted to one synaptic step, it crosses one synapse back to label the neurons that feed it directly.

scenes.tts: Even one-step tracing has a strict limit. In mice, modified rabies virus linked gut lining cells to vagal sensory neurons. Labelling reached them in two of five mice with infected colon nerves. That shows a connection in some animals, not the transmitter or behavioural role.
scenes.caption: Even one-step tracing has a strict limit. In mice, modified rabies virus linked gut lining cells to vagal sensory neurons. Labelling reached them in 2 of 5 mice with infected colon nerves. That shows a connection in some animals, not the transmitter or behavioural role.
scenes.visual: The same schematic two-cell link adapts into a gut-lining cell contacting a vagal sensory neuron. Five simple mouse icons appear with 2 of 5 highlighted beside the label "2 of 5, infected colon nerves" (schematic). Next to the lit pathway, two dimmed labels—"Transmitter?" and "Behaviour?"—remain crossed out.
scenes.narration: Even one-step tracing has a strict limit. In mice, modified rabies virus linked gut lining cells to vagal sensory neurons. Labelling reached them in 2 of 5 mice with infected colon nerves. That shows a connection in some animals, not the transmitter or behavioural role.

scenes.tts: Paired with other tests, circuit mapping unlocked landmark pathways. In nineteen seventy-six, Fernando Nottebohm, Tegner Stokes and Christiana Leonard mapped the adult canary song circuit. Forebrain cluster H V C projects to a second cluster, R A. R A reaches brainstem motor neurons of the vocal organ.
scenes.caption: Paired with other tests, circuit mapping unlocked landmark pathways. In 1976, Fernando Nottebohm, Tegner Stokes and Christiana Leonard mapped the adult canary song circuit. Forebrain cluster HVC projects to a second cluster, RA. RA reaches brainstem motor neurons of the vocal organ.
scenes.visual: The carried left-to-right schematic circuit transforms into a three-station canary song pathway (schematic): a cluster labelled "HVC" sends a glowing tract to "RA", which projects onward to "Vocal motor neurons". Crisp source tag: "Nottebohm, Stokes & Leonard, 1976".
scenes.narration: Paired with other tests, circuit mapping unlocked landmark pathways. In 1976, Fernando Nottebohm, Tegner Stokes and Christiana Leonard mapped the adult canary song circuit. Forebrain cluster HVC projects to a second cluster, RA. RA reaches brainstem motor neurons of the vocal organ.

scenes.tts: In nineteen eighty-nine, Andrew Lumsden and Roger Keynes mapped cranial motor neurons in chick embryos. These neurons drive muscles of the jaw, face and throat. Mapping their origins showed each cranial nerve's motor neurons come from a pair of hindbrain segments.
scenes.caption: In 1989, Andrew Lumsden and Roger Keynes mapped cranial motor neurons in chick embryos. These neurons drive muscles of the jaw, face and throat. Mapping their origins showed each cranial nerve's motor neurons come from a pair of hindbrain segments.
scenes.visual: The schematic circuit morphs into six lined-up embryonic chick hindbrain segments (schematic). Three pairs of segments light up in distinct colours, each pair sending a glowing axon bundle out to schematic labels "Jaw", "Face", and "Throat". Crisp source tag: "Lumsden & Keynes, 1989".
scenes.narration: In 1989, Andrew Lumsden and Roger Keynes mapped cranial motor neurons in chick embryos. These neurons drive muscles of the jaw, face and throat. Mapping their origins showed each cranial nerve's motor neurons come from a pair of hindbrain segments.

scenes.tts: And David Hubel, Torsten Wiesel and Simon LeVay closed one eye in infant macaque monkeys. Tracing stripes in visual cortex showed the open eye's stripes widened while the closed eye's narrowed. Across brains, axon transport turns hidden wiring into maps that physiology can test.
scenes.caption: And David Hubel, Torsten Wiesel and Simon LeVay closed one eye in infant macaque monkeys. Tracing stripes in visual cortex showed the open eye's stripes widened while the closed eye's narrowed. Across brains, axon transport turns hidden wiring into maps that physiology can test.
scenes.visual: The schematic axon bundles shift into alternating eye-input stripes in visual cortex (schematic), fed by axons from left and right eyes. As one eye's input dims, the open eye's stripes widen while the closed eye's stripes narrow. Crisp source tag: "Hubel, Wiesel & LeVay". The stripes then settle into a calm glowing schematic network.
scenes.narration: And David Hubel, Torsten Wiesel and Simon LeVay closed one eye in infant macaque monkeys. Tracing stripes in visual cortex showed the open eye's stripes widened while the closed eye's narrowed. Across brains, axon transport turns hidden wiring into maps that physiology can test.
